articles.title_orig: Redefining Education as a Way of Life (SSIR)
articles.title_zh: Redefining Education as a Way of Life (SSIR)
articles.content_orig:
This article is based on a recent written dialogue between the two authors about the New Education Initiative (NEI), the largest NGO in China, which operates in more than 11,000 schools nationwide. Yongxin Zhu, a Yidan Prize laureate, founded NEI. Kai-ming Cheng is an emeritus professor at The University of Hong Kong and emeritus advisor to the Yidan Prize. The dialogue was conducted in Chinese and comprised more than 80,000 characters .
With a population of more than 1.4 billion people, China has a vast education system: more than 136,300 primary schools, 52,100 junior secondary schools, 15,800 senior secondary schools, and more than 3,000 institutes of higher education. The system has nearly universal attendance at the basic education level and is supported by sophisticated governance. It also has a strong culture in which parents value education highly, teachers work exceptionally hard, and students achieve strong results in international comparisons.
Yet what has held the national system together is examinations, especially public examinations. It is perhaps no exaggeration to say that China is the home of standardized testing. Public examinations were formalized about 1,600 years ago as a mechanism for selecting people for the civil service. At the heart of this system is a paradigm of equal competition that has spread to other countries and become a foundation of civil service systems. Because civil examinations have tested mostly reading and writing, they are often mistakenly regarded as an “education” system. The system has instead created a culture that respects hard work and honors competition while placing less emphasis on innate ability. It has also resulted in a preoccupation with symbolic achievement at the expense of authentic learning.
Although Chinese students perform exceptionally well in international comparisons, the culture has come under heavy public criticism. There is simply no substitute for the examination system, yet its negative effects—including intense pressure, depression, and anxiety among students—are felt across the country. Critics argue that students are too often placed in structured, passive modes of learning. They have few opportunities to think deeply, explore the meaning of what they are learning, or indeed, consider the meaning of life.
That said, many schools are seeking to transform their learning environments so that students can enjoy a more relaxed and meaningful life. Both authors of this article have visited many schools, and Zhu, in particular, visits nearly 100 schools each year. As an academic, he set out to explore the schools in search of breakthroughs. He reads extensively, beginning at around 5 each morning, a habit that has helped him summarize and theorize what he observes on the ground.
Through this work, he has come to believe that breakthroughs in education must begin with students. Above all, education should support students’ well-being, rather than teaching them to equate success with high scores and satisfaction with prizes.
Students need a rich and comprehensive life in which they can grow, and different students will follow different paths in their development. This vision runs counter to the educational paradigm that emerged at the height of the industrial era, in which every student was expected to learn the same things, follow the same processes, and undergo the same assessments.
Over the course of his observations, Zhu found that some schools were doing better than others, despite facing the same examination pressures. The students lived healthy, energetic lives because they enjoyed a harmonious school environment. He observed this phenomenon at the grassroots level, on the front lines where educational innovation takes place.
There is no shortage of theories in education, most of them originating in the West. It is easy to fit what we observe in schools into existing theories, or to build on those theories to propose incremental improvements and, eventually, a new theory that can readily lead to academic recognition. Zhu’s work is distinctive in its purpose: He observes schools not simply to develop theory, but also to find ways to improve schools more broadly.
After years of observation, Zhu has concluded that the real wisdom of education lies on the front lines of schools. He is particularly adept at recognizing the strengths of individual schools, but more importantly, distilling what he has observed into insights that can have meaning for all schools.
This approach to school is especially important at a time when circumstances are changing so rapidly that schools cannot afford to wait for theories to emerge. Young people face a world of unexpected changes and challenges, and they need to develop the agency to shape their own futures. Schools operate in local environments and under diverse conditions, but they want to understand how their work fits into the larger picture.
The NEI not only provides a broad framework to guide schools; it also respects diversity. Its motto, “Providing an Enlightening and Fulfilling Education Life,” requires some explanation.
The original Chinese motto draws on three concepts: “happiness” (幸福), “comprehensiveness” (完), and “education life” (教育生活). These were Cheng’s initial translations. But an in-depth conversation with Zhu revealed deeper meanings behind each term.
First, “happiness” is best understood as students’ well-being. “Happiness” is not a goal in itself. Students must undertake hard work and difficult tasks. Those experiences are essential to their growth. Schools, in turn, must create the conditions for students’ well-being and help them find meaning in their lives. In this sense, happiness is understood broadly, with a long-term view of students’ development.
“Comprehensiveness,” too, is only a partial interpretation of the original term. Chinese schools already provide students with a wide range of activities, and extracurricular activities are often abundant. For Zhu, however, comprehensiveness generally means something more fundamental: students should understand success as something larger than examination scores, and meaning as something beyond winning prizes or gaining admission to prestigious universities. They should have the opportunity to pursue the goal of “becoming a better self.” Zhu emphasizes that this goal will look different for different people. Comprehensiveness is about fulfillment in the broadest sense.
Cheng grappled with how to translate “education life.” He considered “school life” and “learning life,” but found neither satisfactory. His conversations with Zhu made clear that the term refers to a holistic approach to education and the ecology in which students are embedded. It encompasses schools and families, but also the media and society at large. For this reason, “education life” may be worth retaining as the translation, since it captures a distinctive and emerging way of thinking about education.
On reflection, the motto might be rendered as, “Let students enjoy well-being and a fulfilling education life.” It is far from a perfect interpretation but it comes close to capturing the spirit of the original.

articles.title_orig: Sen. Cantwell said Lutnick failed to stop U.S. AI chip exports to China
articles.title_zh: Sen. Cantwell said Lutnick failed to stop U.S. AI chip exports to China
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures slide as Nvidia leads AI stocks lower: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures slide as Nvidia leads AI stocks lower: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia 's stock continued its slide on Monday, after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week amid the fallout from Jensen Huang resigning as CEO.
The company was 3.65% down in premarket trading on Monday as of 7:04 a.m. ET.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8.
It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday.
An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures , as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk, rallied behind him.
Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal.
Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world's most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology's boom.
Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive.
He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.

articles.title_orig: China Confirms Xi, Trump, Putin Trilateral Summit in Shenzhen on November 19: 20 outlets compared
articles.title_zh: China Confirms Xi, Trump, Putin Trilateral Summit in Shenzhen on November 19: 20 outlets compared
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_zh: China stands with the people of the Middle East and Africa, on right side of history: Foreign Ministry
articles.content_orig:
Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.
The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade service developed by Elon Musk's Starlink and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.
Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.
US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.
On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".
"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.
"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try to carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

articles.title_orig: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
articles.title_zh: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
articles.content_orig:
Billionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annual charitable giving from the prior year.
Buffett, 96, converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, and 1,845,000 shares to each of The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and NoVo Foundation — the foundations run by his three children, Susie, Howard and Peter Buffett.
Following the donations, the chairman emeritus of Berkshire still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion.
"Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought," wrote Buffett, who was succeeded as chairman in September by his son Howard, in his annual Thanksgiving message.
The letter was much shorter than his message last Thanksgiving. Charlie Munger, former vice chairman of Berkshire, passed away in November 2023.
Berkshire shares have been on a tear recently, up more than 19% since the start of the fourth quarter and ending last week with four consecutive record high closes. That compares with the S&P 500's decline of 1.2% so far for the fourth quarter. Berkshire has been seen as a safe haven as investors have worried about the AI buildout, corporate drama and geopolitical risk.
The shares are now outperforming the S&P 500 for the year by about 7.5 percentage points.
In his letter, Buffett reiterated that all of his Berkshire shares eventually will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal being to increase the size of the grants each year.
Buffett wrote that the gifts were a signal of his confidence not only in his three children, but also in Berkshire CEO Greg Abel:
"My children have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity...You heard plenty from me in September about my confidence in Berkshire. That confidence is as strong as ever," he said.
Referring to Munger and himself, Buffett added, "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received."
"Warren continues to share his wisdom with us all during this holiday season. His example reflects the kindness he encourages in all of us," said CEO Abel of the letter.
Buffett closes his message with this advice: "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."

President purchased up to $5m of stock before revoking Biden-era rule that limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to China
Donald Trump bought Nvidia stock worth millions of dollars as he made decisions on America’s China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis has found .
In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China.
This rule aimed to strengthen the US’s own chip industry and to protect America from what was widely regarded as a national security threat: the possibility that China might develop superior AI.
In the days before he rescinded the rule, Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate that he bought between $1m (£760,000) and $5m worth of Nvidia stock – a purchase noted in an analysis by the anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy.
He also bought shares in other tech companies, including Apple, Meta and Microsoft.
The diffusion rule would have limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to what has been one of its largest markets: China accounted for about a quarter of the company’s sales between 2010 and 2022. Nvidia’s shares rose in value just after Trump announced the rescission of the rule, and after he had bought the stock.
In December 2025 Trump said he would allow Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China, a decision that was greenlit by the Department of Commerce in January 2026. This was a controversial move. H200s were one of the company’s most advanced chips – six times better than what was available in China at the time, said experts.
The Council on Foreign Relations suggested selling H200s would “supercharge” China’s future AI factories and strengthen the US’s rival.
Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate he made at least three purchases of Nvidia shares in the days after announcing this, all of them between $250,001 and $500,000.
These trades are among Trump’s larger purchases of Nvidia stock, although he appears to have made dozens of transactions involving the chipmaker’s shares since taking office.
DeKleptocracy wrote in its analysis: “While the country debates how a possible Chinese spy may have manipulated White House policy for one AI company, it must grapple with how Trump’s corruption may have motivated him to deliver the entire AI industry’s technology to China.”
after newsletter promotion
The US – and the global economy – have been grappling with revelations that Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s former chief executive, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
Reports have suggested this relationship allowed Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, to obtain billions of dollars worth of Nvidia’s chips, even as other companies struggled.
Trump was twice briefed by US intelligence officials on their conclusions that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset. He did not act on this assessment.
Jensen Huang has been described as a close Trump ally and has met the president a number of times. Nvidia made a $25m contribution to Trump’s ballroom in October 2025, with Huang saying he was “delighted to be a part of it”.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Has Spoken to Allies About Nvidia Return, Report Says
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Has Spoken to Allies About Nvidia Return, Report Says
articles.content_orig:
Allies of Jensen Huang are trying to rally support for the former Nvidia boss to get his job back after resigning last week over a scandal involving extramarital affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy.
SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, are among those backing a campaign to get the AI chip giant's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after the emergence of two affairs, one of whom was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion.
An open letter calling for Nvidia's board to give Huang his job back while an internal  probe is conducted has received more than 175,000 signatures, including Musk and Sweeney, according a website named "Stand with Jensen".
The campaign group said it is made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.
"We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests," the letter said.
Allies of the ex-Nvidia boss wrote they were "concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, this time allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to Financial Times.
The newspaper quoted one ally saying that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being convened to lobby for the former Nvidia boss's reinstatement.
A representative for Jensen Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
While President Donald Trump recently spoke in glowing terms about Huang , the scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The former Nvidia boss has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China .
The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while the Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost," he posted on X.
He later added: "If Jensen gave me his word about compute delivery or I asked for components to be accelerated, he always came through."
If Huang was reinstated, it would face scrutiny from Washington. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at Nvidia's helm.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

articles.title_zh: Tributes as wife and daughter of DUP chairman die hours apart
articles.content_orig:
Sympathies have been expressed to a senior Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) politician following the death of his wife and daughter within hours of each other.
The party said Lord Morrow, who is chairman of the DUP, lost his wife Lady Jennifer Morrow and their daughter Rachel Burrows at the weekend.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that "words cannot adequately express the heartbreak and sorrow felt across our party".
"There are no words that can ease the pain of such an unimaginable loss," he added.
Lord Morrow is a former Stormont minister and a former assembly member for the Fermanagh and South Tyrone constituency.
A funeral notice for his daughter Rachel said she was a married mother of two children. It said she died on Sunday "peacefully surrounded by her loving family".
Robinson added that Lord Morrow's wife and daughter died "within hours of each other" on Sunday.
"On behalf of the Democratic Unionist Party, I extend our deepest sympathy to Maurice, to Rachel's husband John, and to the entire Morrow and Burrows families at this most difficult of times," he said.
"Maurice Morrow has been a rock of strength and support to so many of us through difficult moments in our lives. Now, in his darkest hour, it is our turn to be a rock for him.
"Throughout Jennifer and Rachel's long battles, Maurice has demonstrated extraordinary love and strength."
Speaking at Stormont, Robinson said the last couple of weeks for Lord Morrow would "have been incredibly difficult".
"But to lose your daughter and know how gravely ill your wife is, and to lose your wife some four hours later yesterday, is a deep personal shock and tragedy for him, for his surviving daughter Victoria, for Rachel's husband John and their two children, and for the wider Morrow and Burrows family."
Robinson said that as party chairman for the last 26 years, Lord Morrow has been "steadfast and fundamental to the foundations of the DUP".
"The commitment that runs through us runs through Maurice, and so this time all of us are here as colleagues to pay tribute to Maurice, to offer him comfort and prayers," he added.
Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister also extended his sympathies to Lord Morrow and expressed "sincere Christian condolences".

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Hits Crimean Bridge in Record Drone Strike on Russia
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Hits Crimean Bridge in Record Drone Strike on Russia
articles.content_orig:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine
Ukraine has hit the Kerch Bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.
A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.
In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.
Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.
The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.
after newsletter promotion
Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.
Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including town and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.
Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son in law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title_orig: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
articles.title_zh: India’s next geopolitical hedge against China: Luring Korean shipbuilders to its ports
articles.content_orig:
It's on us. Share your news here.
Posted on November 16, 2026
India’s push to expand domestic shipbuilding and lessen its dependence on China has found an eager partner in Korea, whose shipbuilders are looking for new production bases abroad.
Those complementary needs are driving a burgeoning partnership centered on Thoothukudi, a port city near India’s southern tip, where HD Hyundai plans to build a $4 billion shipyard with Indian state partners. On India’s west coast, Samsung Heavy Industries is backing an Indian yard competing for the country’s first oil tanker orders in decades.
The stakes reach beyond the two countries. China, Korea and Japan accounted for about 93 percent of global shipbuilding in 2024, according to Clarksons Research, and India is spending public money to become the fourth name on that list, with Korean partners instead of Chinese ones.
When India’s shipping minister visited Korea last month, he toured Korean shipyards and explored business opportunities with all three of Korea’s major shipbuilders, underscoring New Delhi’s push to expand its shipbuilding industry.
India’s Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal met HD Hyundai Chairman Chung Ki-sun, Samsung Heavy Industries CEO Choi Sung-an and Hanwha Ocean Executive Vice President Kim Chang-yong to ask for investment and technology transfer during a four-day trip that ended Oct. 28.
The tour was the latest in a series of attempts by New Delhi to import an industry it has not managed to build on its own. India ranks 12th in global shipbuilding and wants to be in the top five by 2047.
For Korean yards that are full at home and losing orders to China, it is a subsidized way to add capacity. The outcome will show whether a shipbuilding industry can be assembled outside East Asia from state funding and borrowed know-how.
About 95 percent of India’s trade by volume moves by sea, the country spends close to $75 billion a year hiring foreign ships, and its own yards held 0.5 percent of the global order book as of Sept. 1, according to the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO).
Indian cabinet earmarked 697.3 billion rupees ($7.4 billion) in September 2025 to lift annual capacity to 4.5 million gross tons by 2047. State-run buyers plan to order 437 vessels worth about 2.2 trillion rupees.
Demand is not the constraint but the ability to build is. Indian yards delivered about 65,000 deadweight tons of ships in the fiscal year through March 2025, roughly a fifth of a single supertanker. Cheap labor does not close the gap. An Indian yard needs 150 to 180 man-hours for work that takes 10 to 15 in Korea, Han Seung-han, an analyst at SK Securities, wrote in a September report.
“A policy of adding capacity does not by itself raise the ability to build ships,” Han wrote. “The capability to run a yard has to come in whole.”
Korean yards face the reverse problem. The industry is in a supercycle, and “domestic production capacity is almost full, with work backed up three to five years,” said Lee Kyu-seok, a senior research fellow at the Export-Import Bank of Korea’s Overseas Economic Research Institute. India, he added, appears to offer “a structure where it is easier to match production costs.”
Nor would Indian yards serve only India. “Shipbuilding is already globalized,” Lee said.
Among the partners India could have chosen, China, the largest builder, seems ruled out. “Because of the border dispute, India does not cooperate with China in strategic industries,” said Kim Kyung-hoon, head of the India and South Asia team at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy.
New Delhi has thawed ties with Beijing, hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping at the BRICS summit in September, but relations remain far from the level needed for industrial cooperation, he said. “Handing shipbuilding subsidies to China is unimaginable.”
Japan’s yards have moved on to specialized vessels, while India wants to start with container ships and large oil tankers, which Korean yards still build, Kim said. “Korea is almost the only partner.”
A similar rivalry looks to be pushing Korea toward India. Chinese yards won 63 percent of global new orders last year and Korean yards 21 percent, according to Clarksons Research. Korean builders now see Southeast Asia and India as partners that can help offset China, an industry representative familiar with the matter said.
“After Southeast Asia, India is the market drawing attention,” the representative said, adding that India is courting Korea’s three major shipbuilders to grow its own industry.
HD Hyundai is leading Korean shipbuilders’ foray into India. When Sonowal met Chung on Oct. 28, the two sides agreed to finish a detailed project report (DPR) on the yard’s cost, size and schedule within six months. The local port authority ordered a feasibility study in September, and site inspections are now underway.
HD Hyundai is to run the yard through a joint venture as its largest shareholder. Until it opens, India plans to place its first orders with HD Hyundai’s yards in Korea and send workers there for training. The partnership began with a Tamil Nadu state agreement in December 2025.
“The specific shareholding structure and investment size of the joint venture are under discussion with the relevant agencies and partners,” HD Hyundai said in a written response to the Korea JoongAng Daily. “However, under the [memorandum of understanding] signed among equity investors on the occasion of the Korea-India summit in April, our baseline is to secure at least 60 percent of the joint venture.”
What HD Hyundai gains is scale it cannot add at home. The yard is planned to turn out about 2.5 million gross tons a year, more than half of the capacity India wants nationwide by 2047. It would be the group’s third overseas base after Vietnam and the Philippines, and subsidies would carry much of the cost: Han estimates that central and state support will cover 45 to 47 percent of the $4 billion bill, leaving HD Hyundai to fund about $2.2 billion.
“We are looking to build a stable production system by securing both Indian domestic orders and global orders,” the company said. “Over the long term, we expect it to diversify our global production system by drawing on India’s abundant work force and growth potential, and to complement the production capacity of our domestic yards.”
Han expects the next round of global orders to center on tankers and bulk carriers, where competing with China comes down to cost. Nearly half of India’s 1,592 ships are more than 20 years old, and most are tankers or bulk carriers, he noted. “It cannot be solved with domestic yards,” Han wrote. “The answer is India, following Vietnam and the Philippines.”
Samsung Heavy Industries has taken a lighter route, lending know-how to an existing Indian yard instead of building one. It signed a cooperation deal in September 2025 with Swan Defence and Heavy Industries. Last month, Swan submitted the lowest bid for up to four product tankers for a venture led by the state-run Shipping Corporation of India, undercutting a Cochin Shipyard bid backed by HD Hyundai. The contract has not been finalized. Hanwha Ocean has so far held talks with state-run Hindustan Shipyard on ship design.
The agreements remain nonbinding, and investment terms and construction dates are still open.
The larger risk lies in India’s follow-through. The yard would take four to five years to build, Kim said, and until then New Delhi and Tamil Nadu have to keep paying subsidies, acquiring land and ordering ships through state firms. “Whether it keeps ordering ships as planned is the question mark,” Kim said. “How binding that cooperation becomes is the biggest question.”
The subsidies also have an end date. India’s shipbuilding aid is scheduled to run until March 2036, so a yard finished around 2031 would have about five years of assured support. “The 20 to 30 percent subsidies offset the cost gap,” Han wrote. “They do not resolve it structurally.”

articles.title_orig: The Investors Set to Win Big in Anthropic’s IPO
articles.title_zh: The Investors Set to Win Big in Anthropic’s IPO
articles.content_orig:
Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain.
Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.
With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.
Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028.
"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."
Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.
By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.
The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.
"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."
Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.
"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.
Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.
It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.
Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.
The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.
Google will be paying particularly close attention.
The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .
"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.
Google didn't provide a comment.
One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.
"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."
Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .
That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.
"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

articles.title_orig: Trump heads to Asia for 2nd high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi amid Nvidia CEO scandal - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump heads to Asia for 2nd high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi amid Nvidia CEO scandal - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Questions remain about the Nvidia CEO's relationship with alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.

He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.

Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."

Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.

"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.

articles.title_orig: War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason
articles.title_zh: War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason
articles.content_orig:
Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.
Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.
Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.
Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.
“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”
In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected secret Iranian missile sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.
His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

articles.title_orig: ‘NATO will collapse’: Russia stalls Ukraine talks, seeks to divide Europe
articles.title_zh: ‘NATO will collapse’: Russia stalls Ukraine talks, seeks to divide Europe
articles.content_orig:
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian drone struck a small house in the northern Ukrainian town of Hlukhiv, burying a nine-year-old boy and his grandmother under the debris.
Two Ukrainian police officers arrived on Saturday to dig them out, apply a tourniquet to the woman’s bleeding arm and take them away in their car.
But a second drone struck their vehicle, killing one of the officers, Mykola Savchenko, who covered the boy with his body, the Ministry of Internal Affairs said.
Such double-tap attacks are Ukraine’s daily reality as the war grinds on to its fifth anniversary. They’re also a metaphor for Russia’s latest attempts to target both Ukraine and those Kyiv has long hoped would help it survive Moscow’s onslaught – NATO and Europe.
On the surface, Russia is engaged in United States-mediated diplomacy. But Russian diplomats who met with US negotiators in Abu Dhabi for trilateral talks involving Moscow, Kyiv and Washington last week presented demands that go far beyond any peace settlement.
Moscow hasn’t agreed to Kyiv’s proposal to freeze the war along the current front lines as Ukraine lacks Western missile interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles and jet drones.
Instead, the Kremlin has shifted the focus of talks from a ceasefire and peace to demands that, if accepted, could dismantle Europe’s post-Cold War security architecture, analysts said.
Russia wants NATO to withdraw its troops from Central and Eastern Europe and ban the bloc’s further expansion, according to leaked documents obtained by The New York Times, The Economist and several Ukrainian media outlets.
Moscow also wants to ink nonaggression pacts with individual European nations, something that may sound alluring to Russia’s neighbours, such as Estonia or Finland.
“Agreements of this kind could be reached, among other things, with individual NATO member states, which would then receive, for instance, additional individual security guarantees” from Moscow, Russian negotiator Alexey Drobinin said at a news conference after the Abu Dhabi talks.
But a string of such agreements could in effect negate NATO’s cornerstone principle to regard any armed attack against one member state as an attack against all of its 32 members.
“NATO will collapse, and European nations will [individually] be face to face with Russia,” said Boris Bondarev, a former Russian diplomat who left his Ministry of Foreign Affairs job in protest against Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Europe will surrender to Russia without firing a single shot in its defence, without losing a single soldier or spending a single shell,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Such individual deals are an absolutely blatant attempt to demolish Europe’s unity, which has already been bursting at the seams, and to undermine NATO’s unity,” said Bondarev, also the author of Time to Win the War, a book that tracks the potential steps needed to reach a peace agreement.
Any nonaggression pacts would most likely include conditions that bar a signatory nation from participating in a future conflict between Russia and another European nation, he said, destroying any potential for collective defence against Moscow.
Russia’s demands were presented to US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff but not to European leaders.
“Russians want to talk to Americans. They don’t want to talk to Europe,” Maria Kucherenko, executive director at the Strategic Intelligence Institute, a think tank in Kyiv, told Al Jazeera.
To Kucherenko, who has for years scrutinised Moscow’s negotiating tactics, the “maximalist” demands continue the Kremlin’s habit of asking for everything.
Russia’s “demands will be maximalist, the way they used to be, and they will be deceptive about the subsequence of steps [towards a peace deal] in their interests. They’ll put politics ahead of security, the way they’ve done all these years,” she said.
Kushner, a real estate developer and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, used the word “very” abundantly to describe the talks.
“These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” Kushner said at a news conference.
To Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Russia’s demands sound otherworldly.
Russian President Vladimir Putin “lives in a different reality”, Zelenskyy wrote on X on Wednesday, adding, “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true.”
“We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100 percent what they want,” Zelenskyy said at a news conference hours later.
A top Ukrainian negotiator decried the “difficulty” of the Abu Dhabi talks.
“This round of talks was one of the most difficult ones. I believe the Russians came with very strict instructions, so it was really hard to ease the discussions,” Davyd Arakhamia, who has taken part in each round of talks since 2022, said on Wednesday.
Stalling the talks will not just weaken Kyiv and demoralise Ukrainians, it may also help Russia buy time until it is politically stronger in Europe’s key nations.
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has pledged to phase out France’s military and financial aid to Ukraine within six months if she wins April’s presidential election. She is currently the frontrunner.
And if Germany’s ruling coalition falls apart amid debates over the budget, debt and economic stagnation, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is positioned to win a snap vote. It leads in national polls and is well ahead of the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
AfD also wants to terminate aid to Ukraine, push for immediate peace talks with Moscow and lift sanctions so Germany can once again buy Russian oil and gas.
If Le Pen and the AfD win, that would compound Ukraine’s struggles with its allies at a time when the Trump administration is already pressuring Kyiv to compromise on its sovereignty.
“We will not be able to withstand the joint position of the European Union and the United States, and a chance to manoeuvre between Washington and Brussels will be lost,” Kyiv-based analyst Aleksey Kusch told Al Jazeera.

articles.title_orig: Relentless Attacks on Ukraine’s Power Grid Threaten to Make Cities Unlivable
articles.title_zh: Relentless Attacks on Ukraine’s Power Grid Threaten to Make Cities Unlivable
articles.content_orig:
When American-led talks to end the war in Ukraine resumed last week in Abu Dhabi , the overriding question was whether Russia intended to give any ground after a nine-month lull in negotiations.
But Russian missiles and drones had already done the talking for Moscow, analysts said . Weeks earlier than expected, Russia has opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter. Daily waves of strikes against Ukraine’s energy system have raised fears that the capital, Kyiv, a city of three million people, could become all but uninhabitable in the coming months.
In the Abu Dhabi talks, an emboldened Russia outlined hard-line demands that stood little chance of gaining acceptance by Ukraine and its European allies. That unbending stance indicated that Russia had no real interest in discussing peace now, because Moscow believes that the winter bombing campaign will strengthen its negotiating position entering the spring.
“They want to come to the table holding our energy system hostage,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said after a recent Russian attack.
The Abu Dhabi talks will be followed by a meeting on Thursday between President Trump, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, at a summit in Shenzhen, China. It was unclear whether the three leaders would discuss the war in Ukraine.
Assaulting infrastructure has become Moscow’s strategy for victory as it has failed for nearly five years to achieve its major objectives in Ukraine. While Russia has tried each winter to knock out the country’s power system and freeze its people into submission, Ukrainian cities are now in their most precarious position of the war. The grid is more fragile after years of strikes, and the Ukrainian military is struggling to protect the system because of dwindling air defenses.

Four special cars from the Seinfeld Collection will be among those displayed from roughly 200 exhibitors. These include a revolutionary 1955 Porsche 550 Spyder, the brand’s first purpose-built racecar.
A Gooding Christie’s auction will feature more than 70 motorcycles from Billy Joel’s collection, with proceeds benefiting the Joel Foundation. articles.title_orig: AI bubble will likely burst and cause a recession by 2028 election, Wall Street’s former top cop says
articles.title_zh: AI bubble will likely burst and cause a recession by 2028 election, Wall Street’s former top cop says
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence boom is a bubble that will likely burst and cause a recession prior to the 2028 presidential election, Gary Gensler, the former top cop on Wall Street, told CNN.
“It’s already a bubble,” Gensler, who was the point person overseeing US capital markets during the Biden administration, said in an interview.
Gensler’s warning comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry following a cascading series of shocks in recent weeks.
Democrats’ stunning midterm victories raised fears among investors of a looming crackdown on the data centers at the heart of the AI buildout. Washington and Wall Street are still feeling the shockwaves caused by the stunning downfall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, the most important person in the industry. And now a critical test looms: Anthropic is attempting to pull off a record-shattering IPO in the face of these headwinds.
Gensler, who led the Securities and Exchange Commission from 2021 until 2025, pointed to the mind-boggling amounts of money – by some estimates $800 billion a year – being plowed into building AI infrastructure.
“History tells us that when you have a new technology and a significant investment…you come to a point where it plateaus. It retrenches,” said Gensler. “The only question is if it’s a soft recession or something more dramatic.”
The comments appear to make Gensler the most senior former federal regulator to publicly warn that an AI-fueled recession may be on the way.
But his words of caution echo similar AI bubble-bursting warnings from prominent individuals on Wall Street and academics, including hedge fund billionaire Ray Dalio , Harvard economist Kenneth Rogoff and investor Mike Novogratz .
Gensler, now a professor at MIT, pointed to past examples of transformative technologies over centuries that experienced powerful downturns after infrastructure was funded in anticipation of revenue.
“That railroad boom-to-bubble was quite an adventure, and it led to really deep recessions, depressions. The 1920s with electricity, the 1990s with the internet,” Gensler said.
With AI, companies have scrambled to sink enormous sums of money into building data centers, buying cutting-edge computer chips and other equipment.
There is a race to build the smartest models and the best chips to cash in on an epic gold rush on Wall Street and to beat China in a high-stakes arms race for tech superiority.
But money is pouring in to this space faster than the ability to turn a profit – an unsustainable mismatch that must eventually come into balance, one way or another.
All of this raises the specter of companies overinvesting and piling on too much debt.
“The Big Tech companies are spending five times more in 2026 than they were just three years ago…It’s just the extraordinary size of it all,” Gensler said.
Nvidia’s financial tentacles reach almost every corner of the AI ecosystem, to the point that the company has been dubbed the central bank of AI, with Huang its chairman – until his sudden exit last week.
It’s not just the spending that worries AI skeptics. It’s how this binge is being funded.
Gensler, who served as chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission during the Obama administration, expressed concern that some of this spending has been hidden from view. He pointed to circular financing and complex, off-balance sheet financing that make it difficult to understand just how much risk is being taken on.
“One might question why all the lenders are lending all this money,” Gensler said. “I think history will show that they loaned too much money, too fast. And that’s the nature of these types of booms that become bursted bubbles.”
The AI boom was built around Jensen Huang. Now what?
So if this boom goes bust, where will the first dominos fall?
Gensler pointed to neoclouds, the specialized cloud-based platforms that lease out massive amounts of specialized supercomputing brainpower to AI developers.
Canary in the coal mine or just a bad apple? CoreWeave debt drama roils Wall Street
The problem is that some of these companies have built their businesses on a mountain of debt and their business models are vulnerable to sudden shifts.
“The major companies will survive. It’s these neocloud companies where we’re going to see some breakage and bankruptcies,” Gensler said.
Elon Musk ominously warned that the 200-plus existing neoclouds will experience “guppy-level death and consolidation.”
“Some will make it through, but not many,” Musk said in a post on X last month.
Of course, not all bursted bubbles cause recessions – and not all of them are severe.
Gensler said he expects the magnitude of this potential downturn to be “as significant as” the dot-com bubble bursting in the early 2000s but not “as harsh as” the subprime mortgage meltdown that led to the 2008 financial crisis.
And just as the Great Recession served as a powerful backdrop to the 2008 race for the White House, Gensler said this potential downturn could arrive at a critical time in the political calendar.
“I think we’re going to have this repricing and a softening of the economy that happens before November 2028,” he said.
Of course, many on Wall Street believe the past few weeks prove how durable the AI boom really is.
AI stocks have lost significant altitude but they have not imploded and investors have not panicked – despite the recent shocks.
“What we’re seeing here is the air coming out of the bubble. It doesn’t have to burst,” said Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research. “I don’t see this as a bubble that bursts. It’s a self-correcting bubble. Every now and then you get a swoon in the AI trade.”
Yardeni, who was the top economist at Deutsche Bank during the bursting of the dot-com bubble, conceded that Gensler’s warning is a “plausible scenario” but added that bubble fears are preventing an unsustainable melt-up.
“If everyone is convinced that AI is a bubble, it probably isn’t. It’s good that people like Gensler are keeping us all grounded because in some ways that reduces the downside,” Yardeni said.
Some of these concerns have helped deflate once-lofty valuation metrics, lowering the risk that stocks become untethered to reality.
Yardeni pointed to how price-to-earnings ratios for chipmakers have tumbled below that of the broader market.
“We’re not looking at 1999-2000 all over again. There is no irrational exuberance in valuations,” he said.
The former SEC chairman said he believes in the “underlying technology” powering AI but still worries capital markets are mispricing it.
Gensler, who grew up on the Chesapeake Bay, likened the current moment to sailing with ominous clouds on the horizon.
“I can’t say exactly when and how stormy,” he said, “but I would be battening down some hatches and making sure you have some proper rain gear.”

Stock futures were mixed Monday morning following a volatile week on Wall Street, as traders await a highly anticipated earnings report from Nvidia and a potentially record-setting public market debut of Anthropic.
Nasdaq-100 futures declined 0.79%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.25%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures gained 21 points, rising almost 0.1%.
Shares in Nvidia were down 1.58% in premarket trading, as the embattled chipmaker prepares to report its third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the company to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"The main task at hand for interim CEO Colette Kress [is to] restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward," wrote Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter."
Another key catalyst is Anthropic's initial public offering. The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
Wall Street is coming off a winning week despite Nvidia's tumble. The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their biggest weekly gains since August, rising more than 2% each.
In Asia, markets closed mostly lower Monday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 dropping 2.42% after third-quarter GDP unexpectedly shrank. South Korea's Kospi slumped 3.59%, leading losses in the region. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.41%. Mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.91% after downbeat key economic data, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index gained 0.49%.
In Europe, the pan-European Stoxx 600 was up 0.12%. The U.K. FTSE 100 rose 0.28%, while France's CAC 40 advanced 0.30%. Germany's DAX was just above the flatline.
Nvidia 's stock fell 1.72% in premarket trading, continuing its slide after losing hundreds of billions in market cap last week amid the fallout from Jensen Huang resigning as CEO.
Nvidia announced Huang was stepping down as CEO on Thursday, amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a spy for China. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday.
Oil prices moved higher on Monday, with Brent crude — the global price benchmark — rising 0.30% to $96.13 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures added 0.49% to $89.03.
The rise comes after two oil tankers reportedly struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters, which cited Iran's Revolutionary Guard. It followed similar reported incidents on Sunday and Monday.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was almost 0.1% higher in early dealmaking, as most continental sectors made gains and major bourses were mixed shortly after 8:10 a.m. in London (3:10 a.m. E.T.).
Healthcare stocks advanced 0.79%, followed by telecommunications, which were up 0.67%, as household goods gained 0.63%. Basic resources shed 1.67%
Among regional bourses, the French CAC 40 led early gains, rising 0.30%, while the U.K. FTSE 100 added 0.22%. Germany's DAX fell 0.10%, and the Italian FTSE MIB was 0.39% down.
European stock markets are expected to start the new trading week in mostly negative territory.
Stoxx 50 futures seen opening almost 0.1% lower, with all of the continent's major bourses in the red.
The French CAC 40 was almost 0.2% down ahead of Monday's session, while the Italian FTSE MIB was about 0.1% lower.
Futures tied to the U.K. FTSE 100 and Germany's DAX were seen opening around the flatline.
Asian tech heavyweights slid on Monday as investors continued to grapple with the fallout from developments at chip giant Nvidia, with former CEO Jensen Huang reportedly mulling a dramatic comeback.
Key Nvidia suppliers Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company all plunged, with SK Hynix down over 5.6%. Samsung and TSMC lost about 3% each.
AI-related stocks in Japan saw larger losses, with Advantest plunging almost 10% and Tokyo Electron falling 5.2%. Softbank Group Corp , a major AI investor, declined 4.2%.
China's economic slowdown worsened in October with retail sales, investment and industrial output all missing economists' estimates, as analysts warn the growing reliance on external drivers is deepening structural imbalances.
